turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was more than one option, I think, near the middle of the screen, and I wasn't quite sure which one was the main one. Something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual hierarchy between the "Continue Shopping" and "Place Order" buttons at the bottom of the screen.
B) The grouping of the different payment fields (Card number, MM/YY, CVV) within the Payment Details box.
C) The placement of the itemized list in the Order Summary compared to the input fields below it.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably A? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: What specifically about the visual styling or placement of those two buttons at the bottom makes it difficult to distinguish which one is the primary action?
turns.a: There was — I think a 'Continue Shopping' button? It looked more prominent than the other one — 'Place Order,' I think. I wasn't sure if 'Continue Shopping' was the main action or if 'Place Order' was the one that was actually the main action. 'Continue Shopping' just seemed more... there. Like it had more weight behind it.

turns.q: What specific visual elements, such as the size or positioning of those two buttons at the bottom, contribute to that sense of "weight" for the 'Continue Shopping' option?
turns.a: I'm not sure it's really a problem — for me specifically. Someone who uses this kind of checkout flow regularly would probably just know which was 'Place Order.' I just... wasn't sure which was the main next step. But that might just be my reading of it.

turns.q: If a developer built this layout exactly as shown, how would that lack of clarity regarding the "main" action play out for someone encountering it for the first time?
turns.a: My eye kept going back to 'Continue Shopping' — scanning it as if it might be the confirmation step. Then I'd re-read both labels. I had to do that a couple of times before I felt sure which was the right one. It's not a big deal — it only takes a moment — but I did have to re-read the whole row. I'm not sure if that's typical.

turns.q: When you had to re-read both labels multiple times to figure out which was the main step, what does that tell you about how the layout currently organizes the priority of these two actions?
turns.a: I genuinely wasn't sure if 'Continue Shopping' was supposed to lead to a confirmation page somehow — like maybe I'd misread the whole flow. I sat there for a moment thinking maybe it was the step that led to a confirmation, which obviously it wouldn't, but that's where I went. It made me second-guess whether I was reading the buttons correctly at all.

turns.q: What would need to be reorganized in this layout for the distinction between "Continue Shopping" and "Place Order" to be clear enough that you wouldn't have to re-read them?
turns.a: I suppose just... make it clearer which button is the main one? Though I'm sure there are reasons it's set up the way it is. It's not really my call to say how the layout should look.

turns.q: If the design team could only change one structural thing before this went to development, what specific change would make it clear enough that you wouldn't have to second-guess which button is the primary action?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' needs to be downgraded visually — made into a text link or a ghost outline, something that reads as secondary, an option rather than an action. And 'Place Order' needs a solid fill color with real contrast — something that immediately reads as 'this is the primary action, this is the step that finishes it.' If those two things were right — 'Continue Shopping' quiet, 'Place Order' prominent — I'd have gone straight to the right button without any hesitation and not needed to re-read anything.
